verdict: The site pages are honest and mostly plain, and three of them (the About story, Contact, Topics/Study) already sound like James. But a careful reader would hear a machine in the marketing layer: about 30 em-dashes, 'honest' 25 times and 'actually' 21, an 'It is not X. It is Y.' habit that peaks on the Believe page, display-size aphorisms on /family, and an About section that recites the style guide. /about also states his title, two different year counts and a book count that /books contradicts. None of it needs new facts to fix; 93 small replacements are listed.

patterns.name: Em-dashes outside quotation
patterns.note: About 30 em-dashes sit in copy a visitor reads, including two in the home page headline. The site's own gate treats the em-dash as an AI tell in James's voice, but that gate does not look at page components, so these were never caught. Printed chapter titles in the book's own table of contents (for example 'Not Persecuted—Seduced') are the book's text and are left alone.

patterns.name: 'Honest' as a self-certifying adjective
patterns.note: 'Honest' or 'honestly' appears 25 times across the library, 8 of them on /tools. The brief allows one per essay. Copy that keeps vouching for its own honesty is the thing a skeptic trusts least.

patterns.name: 'Actually', 'real', and the Tuesday stamp
patterns.note: 'Actually' appears 21 times and 'real' 16. 'On a Tuesday' appears on five surfaces and 'the week / life you are actually living' on three. Once, on /about, 'a Tuesday afternoon' is his. Stamped across the site it becomes a brand tic.

patterns.name: 'It is not X. It is Y.' as the default gait
patterns.note: The governing standard allows this at a genuine hinge. The Believe pitch uses it five times in three paragraphs, /about four times in one band, and the tools page as a description template.

patterns.name: Aphoristic closers and display-size slogans
patterns.note: Short balanced lines set as pull quotes, statement bands, section ledes and card closers. Each could be embroidered on a pillow, and several overclaim.

patterns.name: Fragment stacks and anaphora
patterns.note: Verbless fragments stacked for rhythm ('X remains. Y remain. Z remains.', 'For the ... For the ... For the ...', 'One essay, one idea, one resource.'). The standard ranks developed sentences above these.

patterns.name: Rulebook leakage
patterns.note: Page copy that recites the editorial rules (verdicts, steelmanning, self-implication, 'no altar call') instead of just following them.

patterns.name: Title, years, book count, and PCN stated as credentials
patterns.note: The confirmed rule is never to state his title, years in ministry or book count. /about states all three, with numbers that contradict each other and /books. James has also asked that the Pastors Connection Network stay outside this site.

patterns.name: Formula headings and a shifting narrator
patterns.note: Template headings on the book pages, and a narrator who is 'I' on the home page, 'us' on /subscribe, and 'James' / 'he' elsewhere.

findings.tell: brand language ('the voice', 'carry weight'); no contractions; imperative pillow closer
findings.why: 'The voice' is how an editor talks about James, not how he talks about himself. 'Carry weight' is the brand phrase, and 'Begin where you actually are' is an embroidered closer added after the paragraph has already ended well.
findings.replacement: You may still be deciding whether to trust me. That's the right instinct, and you should keep it. The writing will either hold up for you or it won't, and I'd rather you find that out for yourself than be talked into it.

findings.quote: He does not flinch and he does not flatter. Every objection gets its strongest form before it gets an answer. The atheists are quoted at their most formidable, not their most convenient. This is apologetics written from inside the doubt, by a man who once stood outside the faith and walked away — until the evidence walked after him.
findings.tell: symmetrical pair, rulebook leakage, antithesis, em-dash, chiasmus closer, biography beyond the confirmed facts
findings.why: The most machine-sounding paragraph in the library. Four sentences, four devices: an alliterative balanced pair (flinch/flatter), the editorial steelman rule stated as a selling point, a 'most X, not most Y' antithesis, and a chiastic closer (walked away / walked after) hung on a dash. 'Stood outside the faith and walked away' also implies he once left the faith, which is not in the confirmed biography (he came to faith as an adult from atheism).
findings.replacement: Every objection is stated the way the people who hold it would state it, and the atheists are quoted at their strongest. The book was written by a man who was an atheist before he was a Christian and still remembers how the objections sound from that side.

findings.quote: He came to faith from atheism. He did not arrive by feeling his way there.
findings.why: The biography is the headline, used as the reason to buy, and the second sentence is a negation set up only to be knocked down.
findings.replacement: James Bell came to faith from atheism, and he got there by argument more than by feeling.

findings.quote: It is not a book that asks you to stop thinking. It is a book that asks you to keep going.
findings.tell: 'It is not X. It is Y.' closer
findings.why: The fifth antithesis in three short paragraphs. Shortened and contracted it can stay as the one earned turn.
findings.replacement: It doesn't ask you to stop thinking. It asks you to keep going.

findings.quote: This is not a book about who to vote for. It is a book about who you worship.
findings.tell: 'It is not X. It is Y.' used twice in one pitch
findings.why: The pitch opens with the same construction ('not mainly being persecuted. It is being seduced'), which is the book's real thesis and should keep it. Twice in 120 words is a tic.
findings.replacement: This book won't tell you who to vote for. It asks who you worship.

findings.quote: turns it back on the reader: the question is not whether earlier generations were blind, but where ours is.
findings.why: The pitch already opens ('was not a monster. That is the point.') and closes ('is not the past. It is the face looking back.') on antithesis. This middle one is the one to lose.
findings.replacement: turns it back on the reader, who has to ask where our own generation is blind.

findings.quote: A rule of life is not a performance contract. It is a trellis. Choose sustainable practices across prayer, Scripture, rest, community, mission, and the body, and settle on a pattern you can actually keep on an ordinary week.
findings.tell: 'It is not X. It is Y.' with a stock metaphor; 'sustainable'; 'actually'
findings.why: The trellis line is the standard rule-of-life metaphor from every book on the subject, delivered in the exact 'not X. It is Y.' shape. Generic Christian content.
findings.replacement: A rule of life is a trellis, something to grow along. Choose practices across prayer, Scripture, rest, community, mission, and the body, and settle on a pattern you can keep on an ordinary week.

findings.replacement: Fifteen questions across

findings.quote: I have pastored First Baptist Church of Fenton, Michigan for twelve years. I put that first not as a line on a resume but because it is the room where everything here gets tested.
findings.tell: states years in ministry; 'not X but Y'; protests too much
findings.why: States a number of years (twelve) that the same page contradicts further down (fifteen), and then explains that it isn't bragging, which is what a résumé line does. The next two sentences already hold a real antithesis (quiet study / hospital visits) that earns its place.
findings.replacement: I pastor First Baptist Church of Fenton, Michigan, and that's the room where everything here gets tested.

findings.quote: Twelve years in that room will take the abstraction out of almost anyone.
findings.why: Second statement of the unconfirmed number. The sentence is good without it.
findings.replacement: That room will take the abstraction out of almost anyone.

findings.quote: Not to send Americans to do their work for them, and not to hand them a translated version of our assumptions. To put real training in the hands of the men already there, who already know the language and the terrain and the cost, and who will still be there long after any visitor has gone home.
findings.tell: 'Not X, and not Y. To Z.' fragment stack; 'real'
findings.why: Two verbless fragments in the 'Not / not / To' pattern. The thought is his and worth keeping; it only needs subjects and verbs.
findings.replacement: The aim isn't to send Americans to do their work for them or to hand them a translated version of our assumptions. It's to put training in the hands of the men already there, who know the language and the terrain and the cost, and who will still be there long after any visitor has gone home.

findings.quote: LiveWell is not therapy, and it is not Christian self-help. It is not a place that hands you something to think so you can stop thinking. It is closer to a writing desk — where a pastor with {SITE_STATS.yearsInMinistryWord} years of mistakes behind him and five sons in front of him tries to think honestly, out loud, about what it actually means to follow Jesus in a country that has mostly forgotten what his kingdom was ever about.
findings.tell: triple negation then reveal; em-dash; years in ministry; 'honestly' + 'actually'; behind/in-front balance; self in third person
findings.why: Three 'is not' statements building to an 'It is closer to' reveal across a dash, with 'honestly' and 'actually' in the same clause. It renders 'fifteen years' on a page that says 'twelve years' twice. He speaks of himself as 'a pastor ... him' one section after writing 'I'.
findings.replacement: LiveWell isn't therapy and it isn't Christian self-help. It won't hand you something to think so you can stop thinking. It's closer to a writing desk, where a pastor with plenty of mistakes behind him and five sons in front of him tries to think out loud about what it means to follow Jesus in a country that has mostly forgotten what his kingdom was about.

findings.quote: The faith is handed down on purpose, at the table, or it is not handed down at all.
findings.why: A display-size absolute ('or not at all') that is false on its face for the reader this site is written toward: James himself was raised without a father and came to faith as an adult. It reads as a slogan, and to a single parent or a convert it reads as a verdict on them.
findings.replacement: The faith gets handed down on purpose, usually at a table, by the people a child lives with.

findings.quote: <PullQuote>The household is the first church a child ever attends.</PullQuote>
findings.tell: pillow aphorism set as a pull quote
findings.why: Could be printed on a church-lobby canvas unchanged. It is the second display-size epigram on the page and adds nothing the sections around it do not say.

findings.quote: The oldest way a family has ever learned the faith.

findings.replacement: Families have learned the faith by question and answer for centuries.

findings.quote: The work no one applauds, done where no congregation watches. Scripture for the real moments, plus writing and tools for the long obedience of raising children who can carry weight.

findings.why: A balanced verbless opener ('no one applauds / no congregation watches'), then 'the long obedience' (Eugene Peterson's phrase, uncredited) and the brand's 'carry weight'. Nothing here is a thing James would say to a tired parent across a table.
findings.replacement: Most of parenting happens where nobody sees it. Here is Scripture for the hard moments, plus writing and tools for the long work of raising children.

findings.quote: A home is built on a covenant before it is built on anything else. Writing and a real assessment for the marriage your family is standing on.
findings.why: 'X before it is anything else' is a template sentence, and 'a real assessment' implies others are fake.
findings.replacement: Your family stands on your marriage, so start there. Writing and a self-check for the marriage your family is standing on.

findings.quote: Faith does not survive on what alone. A teenager needs the why. Honest answers to the hard questions — the resurrection, the Bible, suffering, science, other religions, and doubt itself.
findings.why: The what/why turn is wordplay that needs a second read, followed by self-certified 'honest answers' and a dash list.
findings.replacement: A teenager needs to know why we believe, and knowing what we believe isn't enough. Answers to the hard questions about the resurrection, the Bible, suffering, science, other religions, and doubt.

findings.quote: Same voice, different rooms.
findings.why: A two-beat closer of the kind the brief bans at paragraph ends.
findings.replacement: It's the same person in each place.

findings.quote: What I want is simple to say and long to do.
findings.why: 'Simple to say / long to do' is symmetry for its own sake; the list that follows makes the point.
findings.replacement: What I want is simple to say.

findings.why: 'Seminary-level depth in kitchen-table language' is a tagline in the X-in-Y shape, followed by '20 books ... 6 layers' in product-spec numerals.
findings.replacement: Twenty books of the Bible in plain language, each with six layers of analysis:

findings.quote: The front door to Scripture's wisdom for the place no rule reaches:
findings.tell: literary image where a plain phrase belongs

findings.quote: The deepest verse tool on the site.
findings.why: A superlative about the site's own tool, as a verbless closer.

findings.quote: In a time of political panic, rising tribalism, and growing confusion inside the church, many believers have quietly begun to place their practical trust in power, policy, and national strength rather than in Christ. The language of faith remains. The rituals remain. The worship remains. But the heart has moved.
findings.tell: 'In a time of' opener; two tidy triplets; anaphora stack with a turn
findings.why: Opens with a cousin of the forbidden 'in today's world' and an adjective-noun triplet (political panic, rising tribalism, growing confusion), then a second triplet (power, policy, national strength), then 'X remains. Y remain. Z remains. But ...'. Every sentence is a formula.
findings.replacement: Many believers have quietly begun to place their practical trust in power, policy, and national strength rather than in Christ. The language of faith is still there, and so are the rituals and the worship, but the heart has moved.

findings.quote: LiveWell is for the person whose faith has grown larger than the answers they were handed as a child. For the pastor who is quietly running on empty. For the husband and wife still keeping a promise they are no longer sure they understand. For the skeptic who keeps reading the words of a faith they have not decided to trust.
findings.tell: anaphora run as fragments ('For the ... For the ... For the ...')
findings.why: Three verbless 'For the' fragments. The people named are right and specific; the stack is what sounds generated. One sentence carries all four.
findings.replacement: LiveWell is for the person whose faith has grown larger than the answers they were handed as a child. It's for the pastor who is quietly running on empty, for the husband and wife still keeping a promise they're no longer sure they understand, and for the skeptic who keeps reading the words of a faith they haven't decided to trust.

findings.quote: Written for pastors carrying the weight. One essay, one sermon-prep idea, one resource. From inside the room where the work actually happens.
findings.tell: brand motif; 'one, one, one' fragment; 'actually'; verbless closer
findings.why: Three fragments, no sentence. 'Carrying the weight' and 'inside the room where the work actually happens' are the brand's stock phrases. (Shown on the pastors' pages, not the home page.)
findings.replacement: For pastors. Each letter has an essay, a sermon-prep idea, and a resource, written by a pastor in the middle of the same work.

findings.quote: Seven essays sent over four weeks. The ones I'd hand a skeptical friend first. No conversion bait. Real questions, real arguments.
findings.tell: fragment stack; 'No X.'; 'Real X, real Y'
findings.why: Four fragments ending on 'Real questions, real arguments', the doubled-adjective closer. 'The ones I'd hand a skeptical friend first' is his and should stay.
findings.replacement: Seven essays sent over four weeks, the ones I'd hand a skeptical friend first. Nobody will push you for a decision.

findings.quote: It is really all one project: taking the depth of theology and putting it back in contact with the weight of an ordinary life.
findings.why: The site tagline ('the depth of theology ... the weight of everyday life') recited as the paragraph's closing reveal.
findings.replacement: It's all one project, really. I'm trying to put theology back in contact with ordinary life.

findings.quote: { name: "It ends on a verdict, not a recap", def: "The last paragraph does not restate the argument. It names what is left once the evidence is on the table, in a few words, and lets you carry it out of the room with you." }
findings.why: This is the editorial style guide printed as page copy: 'verdict', 'evidence', 'does not restate', 'carry it out'. The brief names any use of 'verdict' in prose as an AI tell. A writer does not tell a reader how his last paragraphs work.
findings.replacement: { name: "It doesn't end with a summary", def: "I don't wrap things up at the end. The last paragraph says what's still true after everything else has been said, and I leave it with you." }

findings.quote: { name: "The writer is inside it", def: "When a piece names what the church has gotten wrong, I am part of the church that got it wrong. When it names what pastors tend to hide, I am a pastor who has hidden it. I am not pointing from across the room." }
findings.tell: rulebook leakage; self-implication announced; restating closer
findings.why: The brief asks that he implicate himself 'by doing it, not by announcing it'. The heading speaks of 'the writer' in the third person, and the last sentence restates the two before it as a slogan.
findings.replacement: { name: "I'm inside it", def: "When a piece names what the church has gotten wrong, I'm part of the church that got it wrong. When it names what pastors tend to hide, I'm a pastor who has hidden it." }

strengths: /about, 'My story in my own words' is the most human writing in the library: 'I have been at the same church long enough to have buried people I loved and married their children' and 'usually on a week when I did not feel qualified to answer' could only be him.
HOME_WHO (client/src/lib/positioning.ts) is plain, contracted and specific: 'I'm James Bell, a pastor, Susanna's husband, and dad to five sons.' Biography is stated once and not leaned on.
/contact is exactly the 'quick practical message' register: says what is known, gives the 988 line and Find Help, stops.
/topics and the home page doors describe what is behind each link in ordinary words with real counts (1,189 chapters, 'about ten minutes long') and no selling.

/study is the cleanest long page: 'You did not start the faith. You were handed it.' is an antithesis at a real hinge, and it says plainly that verse notes are finished only for Genesis and the Gospels.
/books hero: 'which is less than the coffee you would read it over' and 'I took the rest of the shelf down to rewrite it in my own hand' sound like a person telling the truth about his own shelf.
No Forbidden Language word or phrase appears anywhere in the library (literal search of every term), and there is no exclamation point in any visible copy.
/about band 'The church, the network...': 'written around hospital visits and budget meetings, after funerals' is concrete and earned; it should survive every edit.
for_james: About page numbers contradict each other and the Books page. /about says 'twelve years' twice and renders 'fifteen years' once (SITE_STATS.yearsInMinistryWord), says 'Author of 21 books' twice, the book-page bio says 'more than twenty books', and /books says 'Three books. Every word mine.' and that the rest were taken down. Tell us one true figure for each, or confirm they should all come off (the replacements here remove them).

You asked on 2026-11-17 to keep the Pastors Connection Network outside this site. It is still named in the home page introduction (HOME_WHO, which you chose on 2026-10-14: 'I founded the Pastors Connection Network'), in a full paragraph and an outbound link on /about, in the About search description and structured data ('nearly 18,000 pastors'), in the bio under two book pages, in the pastors' newsletter pitch, and by implication on /speaking ('A network of pastors who have been through the same'). Say whether a one-line mention with a link out is acceptable or whether every mention goes.

The home page headline you chose has two em-dashes ('Learning to follow Jesus — and live well — in post-Christian America.'). The same sentence without them is already your site description. Approve the plain version?

Three /about passages may be yours word for word (a code note says the page reuses your sentences): 'My story in my own words', 'The heart behind it', and 'How the writing works'. The story section reads as you and is left alone. 'How the writing works' reads like the style guide; if you wrote it, say so and we will only contract it, not rewrite it.

Believe's pitch says you 'once stood outside the faith and walked away — until the evidence walked after him.' That can be read as having left the faith and returned. The confirmed fact is that you came to faith as an adult from atheism. The replacement removes the ambiguity; if there is a truer sentence only you can write, it belongs here.

The home page needs one detail only you can supply to stop sounding like a site description: what a real question across your desk sounded like. /about already has it in general form ('something I had to figure out for an actual person sitting across from me'). We have not invented one.
/speaking offers 'Writing and ghostwriting' on the same site whose Books page says 'Every word mine.' A careful reader may notice. Keep, reword, or drop?
You said no membership fee. Nothing in this library asks for one, but the three books are sold at $8.99 and /books says so plainly. Confirm that book sales stay.

Your saved Substack profile and VOICE-JAMES-BELL.md disagree in a few places; the voice document was followed. The profile asks for 2-4 sentence paragraphs, 'stacked landing lines', 'contrast lines', three numbered applications, and 'one line the reader screenshots' in every piece; the voice document ranks developed paragraphs above fragment stacks and allows one earned verdict, not a slogan per piece. The profile also speaks of paid content that 'justifies the subscription' and names a .com address; neither matches the site now.

Political balance: nothing in this library criticises one side only. The When God Bless America blurb says it is 'not a case for the other party', and the tools page pairs the scorecard and the biblical-government tool against both parties. No change needed.

Crisis paths are present where they should be: the 988 line and Find Help on /contact, a Find Help line at the foot of the home page, /help first under 'Help in a hard season' on /resources, and 'safety first' on the marriage card on /family.

Four constants in client/src/lib/positioning.ts are no longer used anywhere (PRIMARY_HEADLINE, PRIMARY_KICKER, PRIMARY_SUBHEAD, PRIMARY_SUBHEAD_SHORT). They carry the old voice ('New essays weekly', em-dashes, 'forming people who can carry weight'). A later pass can delete them so nobody reuses them.
